rv.q: All these years later, the question remains at the heart of The Who’s Tommy, and we can answer, with great pleasure, loud and clear.

Everything about this exhilarating production shakes you awake and leaves you buzzed: Knockout singing, superbly inventive stagecraft and a star-making performance from 24-year-old Ali Louis Bourzgui as the Pinball Wizard that’s the most exciting New York stage debut in years.
...brings an intoxicating energy to the story of a boy who survives trauma
“Tommy” offers the flip side, a musical explanation of what parents, or a wicked uncle, or a bullying cousin did to us at a vulnerable age.

If the first 10 minutes of a show are supposed to rope you in, “The Who’s Tommy” dares you to need more than 10 seconds. Director Des McAnuff’s revival staging of the electric rock opera he co-wrote explodes onto the Nederlander Theatre stage in a paroxysm of booming sound, blinding light and crackling projections
On its own terms, it’s often sensational.
Bourzgui has something about him that feels un-modern
The Who's Tommy feels like a show that's been waiting decades to be properly realized on Broadway, and this revival finally gives it the spectacular staging it deserves.
A tale of sensory deprivation told through sensory overload makes counterintuitive sense.

Maybe if you'd missed the '70s, when The Who's exceptional album stirred the hearts of kids making enough noise to change the world, you wouldn't care that this production of "Tommy" is basically for old people, and not for a new generation.
But McAnuff and Townshend’s dramatization insists we’re watching a story that does make sense, and then refuses to create that sense.

However loudly and well the performers sing, however frenziedly they dance Lorin Latarro’s dystopian choreography, they rarely surface from the production’s flooding of the senses with any expressiveness intact.
This production creates transcendent enjoyment.
It had me from start to finish, and it’s an amazing journey I’d love to take again.

Truth be told, I was not expecting to be as bowled over by this story, or this revival, as I was. But there’s no arguing with talent, and with so much prowess on and off the stage, Tommy is an electric paean to rock immortality, and talent wherever one can find it.
I appear to have written the word 'thrilling' about 20 times – including at least four times during the breathtaking opening sequence alone.
Tommy’s saga delivers a pointed and potent take on trauma, fame, and individuality that resonates and speaks directly to today.
Indeed, all the boxes have been checked by the thrillingly visceral and gloriously (and loudly) sung new production of the classic 1969 rock opera “The Who’s Tommy,” now at the Nederlander Theatre.
For anyone else, it will be quite the theatrical experience, a rock opera that truly earns its reputation as the genuine article.
Now, The Who's Tommy carries that torch forward in its own radical, one-of-a-kind adventure that truly has to be seen to be believed.
Tommy grabs you and never lets you go
But in the new production, helmed by the original director and co-librettist Des McAnuff, those songs have lost none of their appeal.
In fact, I suspect those who have enjoyed previous incarnations of “Tommy” will find much to like here.
While it certainly aspires to deeper meaning, The Who’s Tommy is, ultimately, a feverish ode to excess, both entertaining and empty, despite serious subject matter that shouldn’t yield either result.
It just feels inessential to me, a revival taking us on one more hero’s journey without a lot of sustaining detail.

Some tableaux are breathtaking; others are rather pedestrian, especially when Nigrini’s projections recede and McAnuff’s direction relies on Sarafina Bush’s unimaginative costumes and Lorin Latarro’s equally mundane choreography.
It’s as if our current fallible AI was given rein to put on a production yielding no heart and humanity.
The main thing is that Pete Townshend’s music and lyrics have never sounded better.

cn.t: This thrilling revival delivers sensory overload with electrifying rock performances and dazzling visuals, though critics split on whether the spectacle compensates for a story that still makes little sense decades later.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
